label: thm:AM
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:AM}
Let \(R\) be regular local analytic of dimension \(n\), let
\(0\ne Q\subsetneq R\), and set \(q=\dim R/Q\). Then
\begin{align}
c_i(Q;R)&=0\quad\text{if }i<n-\ell(Q)\text{ or }i>q,
\label{eq:AM-vanishing}\\
c_q(Q;R)&=
\sum_{\substack{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Min}(Q)\\\dim R/\mathfrak p=q}}
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(QR_{\mathfrak p};R_{\mathfrak p})\,
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(R/\mathfrak p).\label{eq:AM-assoc}
\end{align}
If \(Q\) is equimultiple, only \(c_q(Q;R)\) can be
nonzero. In particular, if \(Q\) is primary to the maximal
ideal, then
\[
(c_0(Q;R),\ldots,c_n(Q;R))=(e_{\mathrm{HS}}(Q;R),0,\ldots,0).
\]
head: environment
name: Achilles--Manaresi

title: Proof
body_md:
These are parts (1), (3), and (5) of \cite[Theorem~3]{AM}.
Regularity supplies the dimension formula required in the
associativity statement. Thus its highest-dimensional associated
primes are exactly the primes displayed in \eqref{eq:AM-assoc}.
head: environment

label: def:segre
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:segre}
The Segre numbers of \(Q\) at the origin are
\[
e_j(Q,Z)=\operatorname{mult}_0\Lambda_j(Q,Z),\qquad 1\leq j\leq m,
\]
for a sufficiently general choice in
\eqref{eq:segre-cycle-recursion}.
head: environment
name: Segre numbers

label: def:generic-le
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:generic-le}
Fix linear coordinates \(\mathbf x\) on \(\mathbb C^n\). There is a
nonempty Zariski-open subset \(\mathcal U_f\subset\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb C)\)
on which the coordinates \(M\mathbf x\) are sufficiently general
and all the L\^e numbers at the origin have constant values.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generic-le}
\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f)=\lambda^i_{f,M\mathbf x}(0),\qquad
M\in\mathcal U_f,\quad 0\leq i\leq n-1.
\end{equation}
The open set may be shrunk without changing these values.
head: environment
name: Generic L\^e numbers

label: rem:generic-identification
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:generic-identification}
For the ambient Jacobian ideal,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:le-segre-c}
\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f)=e_{n-i}(J(f);\mathbb C^n)=c_i(J(f)),
\qquad 0\leq i\leq n-1.
\end{equation}
The first equality identifies the generic L\^e construction with
the Segre construction for the gradient ideal; see
\cite[p.~346]{AM}, \cite{GG,Massey95}. The second equality is
\eqref{eq:segre-c}. This does not identify the L\^e numbers in
every admissible or prepolar coordinate system with Segre numbers.
head: environment
name: Generic L\^e numbers and Segre numbers

label: rem:isolated-identification
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:isolated-identification}
If \(\Sigma(f)=\{0\}\), then \(J(f)\) is a parameter ideal in
the regular local ring \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,0}\). Hence
\[
\mu(f)=\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,0}/J(f)
=e_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(f);\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,0}),
\]
and
\[
\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f)=e_n(J(f))=\mu(f),\qquad
\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f)=0\quad(i\geq1).
\]
In fact \(\lambda^0_{f,\mathbf w}(0)=\mu(f)\) in every
coordinate system for which the construction is defined
\cite[Example~3.11]{MasseyNotes}.
head: environment
name: Isolated singularities

label: lem:units
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:units}
If \(v\) is a holomorphic unit, then
\(\overline{J(vf)}=\overline{J(f)}\). Consequently the Segre
numbers and generic L\^e numbers of \(vf\) and \(f\) agree.
head: environment
name: Independence of a unit factor

title: Proof
body_md:
The analytic curve criterion gives
\(f\in\overline{\mathfrak m J(f)}\): along an analytic arc through
the origin, differentiating \(f\) along the arc proves the
required order inequality. By the Leibniz rule,
\(J(vf)\subseteq\overline{J(f)}\). Applying the same argument
to \(v^{-1}\) proves the reverse inclusion of integral closures.
Segre numbers are invariant under integral closure
\cite{GG,AR}; use \eqref{eq:le-segre-c} for generic L\^e numbers.
head: environment

label: thm:ideal-lex
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ideal-lex}
For proper nonzero ideals \(K\subseteq L\) of a regular local
analytic ring \(R\),
\[
\mathbf e(K;R)\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbf e(L;R).
\]
head: environment
name: Cid-Ruiz--Polini--Ulrich

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cite[Corollary~6.5]{CPU}. A regular local analytic ring is
equidimensional and universally catenary. That paper uses
codimension indexing: its \(c_j\), for \(j\geq1\), is our
\(e_j\); its codimension-zero term is zero for the nonzero
ideals under consideration.
head: environment

label: lem:free
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:free}
Let \(F:(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C^n,0)\) be finite of degree \(d\).
Then \(B\) is free of rank \(d\) over \(A\). For every
\(\mathfrak m\)-primary ideal \(Q\subset A\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:primary-degree}
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(QB;B)=d\,e_{\mathrm{HS}}(Q;A).
\end{equation}
More generally, the freeness assertion and
\eqref{eq:primary-degree} remain valid for a Cohen--Macaulay
source of dimension \(n\) and a smooth target, with \(d\)
interpreted as the generic module rank.
head: environment
name: Freeness and primary multiplicity

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(F\) is finite, \(B\) is finite over \(A\) and
\(\sqrt{\mathfrak m B}=\mathfrak n\). The images of a regular system of
parameters of \(A\) form a system of parameters of \(B\).
Cohen--Macaulayness makes it a \(B\)-regular sequence. Hence
\(\operatorname{depth}_A B=n\); the Auslander--Buchsbaum
formula over the regular ring \(A\) gives
\(\operatorname{pd}_A B=0\). A finite projective module over
the local ring \(A\) is free, and its rank is \(d\).

For every \(k\geq1\),
\[
B/Q^kB\cong(A/Q^k)\otimes_A B\cong(A/Q^k)^{\oplus d}
\]
as \(A\)-modules. Both residue fields are \(\mathbb C\), so the
\(A\)-length and \(B\)-length of a finite-length \(B\)-module
are equal. Comparing the leading Hilbert--Samuel coefficients
proves \eqref{eq:primary-degree}.
head: environment

label: lem:graph
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: A graph multiplicity bound

label: eq:parameter-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Put \(t=\dim A/Q=\dim B/QB\), where equality follows from
finiteness and faithful flatness. We first record a parameter
inequality. If \((R,\mathfrak a)\) has dimension \(D>0\),
\(z\in\mathfrak a\), and \(\dim R/(z)=D-1\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:parameter-bound}
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(R/(z))\geqe_{\mathrm{HS}}(R).
\end{equation}
Indeed, the right-exact sequence
\[
R/\mathfrak a^k\xrightarrow{\cdot z}R/\mathfrak a^{k+1}
\longrightarrow R/(\mathfrak a^{k+1}+zR)\longrightarrow0
\]
gives
\(H_{R/(z)}(k)\geq H_R(k)-H_R(k-1)\), where
\(H_R(k)=\lambda_R(R/\mathfrak a^{k+1})\).
Comparison of leading coefficients proves
\eqref{eq:parameter-bound}, including the case \(D=1\).

Now set
\[
T=\mathbb C\{y_1,\ldots,y_n,x_1,\ldots,x_n\}/
Q\mathbb C\{y_1,\ldots,y_n,x_1,\ldots,x_n\}.
\]
Then \(\dim T=t+n\), \(e_{\mathrm{HS}}(T)=e_{\mathrm{HS}}(A/Q)\), and
\[
T/(y_1-F_1(x),\ldots,y_n-F_n(x))\cong B/QB.
\]
The \(n\) graph equations cut dimension by \(n\); every
successive quotient therefore cuts dimension by one. Applying
\eqref{eq:parameter-bound} successively proves the lower bound
in \eqref{eq:graph-bound}.

For the upper bound, use \(\mathfrak m B\subseteq\mathfrak n\) and the
fact that \(B/QB\) is a free \(A/Q\)-module of rank \(d\).
Length comparison gives
\[
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(\mathfrak n;B/QB)\leqe_{\mathrm{HS}}(\mathfrak m B;B/QB)
=d\,e_{\mathrm{HS}}(\mathfrak m;A/Q),
\]
as required.
head: environment

label: prop:flat-cycles
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:flat-cycles}
Let \(0\ne J\subsetneq A\), and put \(I=JB\). A common
sufficiently general sequence of linear combinations of generators
of \(J\), and their pullbacks, computes the Segre numbers of
\(J\) and \(I\). For these choices the cycles satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-cycles}
\Lambda_j(I,\mathbb C^n)=F^*\Lambda_j(J,\mathbb C^n),
\qquad 1\leq j\leq n,
\end{equation}
where \(F^*\) denotes flat pullback of cycles, including
multiplicities.
head: environment
name: Pullback of Segre cycles

title: Proof
body_md:
Use a fixed set of generators of \(J\) and its image in \(B\).
The good coefficient matrices for each Segre construction contain
a nonempty Zariski-open subset of the same matrix space. Their
intersection is nonempty. Choose a matrix in this intersection.

Flat pullback commutes with intersection by a Cartier divisor.
Moreover, a component of the inverse image of an irreducible
cycle component maps onto that component: the map is finite flat
of relative dimension zero. Such an inverse-image component is
contained in \(V(I)\) exactly when its image is contained in
\(V(J)\). Consequently flat pullback commutes with both parts
of the decomposition \eqref{eq:segre-cycle-recursion}.
Starting from \(F^*[\mathbb C^n]=[\mathbb C^n]\), induction gives
\(P_j(I)=F^*P_j(J)\) and \eqref{eq:flat-cycles}.
This argument concerns cycles, not merely their reduced supports;
ramification multiplicities are retained throughout.
head: environment

label: thm:flat-segre
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Finite-flat Segre comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose compatible cycles as in Proposition~\ref{prop:flat-cycles}
and write
\[
\Lambda_j(J)=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha[V(\mathfrak p_\alpha)],
\qquad \dim A/\mathfrak p_\alpha=n-j.
\]
The flat pullback of \([V(\mathfrak p_\alpha)]\) is the
fundamental cycle of \(B/\mathfrak p_\alpha B\). By the
associativity formula for Hilbert--Samuel multiplicity,
\begin{align*}
e_j(J;A)&=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\,e_{\mathrm{HS}}(A/\mathfrak p_\alpha),\\
e_j(I;B)&=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\,e_{\mathrm{HS}}(B/\mathfrak p_\alpha B).
\end{align*}
Lemma~\ref{lem:graph}, applied term by term, proves
\eqref{eq:flat-segre-bounds}. For \(j=n\), the only possible
component downstairs is \([0]\), and its flat pullback has
multiplicity \(\lambda_B(B/\mathfrak m B)=d\). This gives
\eqref{eq:j-degree}.
head: environment

label: rem:false-degree
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:false-degree}
Freeness gives the expected factor \(d\) when the auxiliary
filtration upstairs is the \(\mathfrak m B\)-adic filtration.
It does not identify that filtration with the
\(\mathfrak n\)-adic filtration used in the definition of \(c_i(I;B)\).
Although \(\sqrt{\mathfrak m B}=\mathfrak n\), this does not imply that
\(\mathfrak m B\) is a reduction of \(\mathfrak n\).

For example, let \(F(u,v)=(u,v^d)\), with \(d>1\), and
\(J=(y_1)\). Then \(I=(u)\) and
\[
e_1(J;A)=e_1(I;B)=1,
\]
not \(e_1(I;B)=d\). Here \(\mathfrak m B=(u,v^d)\), whose
Hilbert--Samuel multiplicity is \(d\), whereas
\(e_{\mathrm{HS}}(\mathfrak n;B)=1\). Thus these primary ideals cannot have
the same integral closure. The exact formula that survives for
all ideals is \eqref{eq:j-degree}, not an exact formula at
every index.
head: environment
name: Why the degree formula does not hold at every index

label: lem:first-coefficient
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The first possible coefficient under inclusion

title: Proof
body_md:
Every minimal prime of \(L\) with quotient dimension \(s\)
is a minimal prime of \(K\) with that dimension, because
\(K\subseteq L\) and their heights agree. At such a prime
\(\mathfrak p\), both localized ideals are primary and
\[
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(KR_{\mathfrak p};R_{\mathfrak p})
\geqe_{\mathrm{HS}}(LR_{\mathfrak p};R_{\mathfrak p}).
\]
Formula~\eqref{eq:AM-assoc}, together with the nonnegative
contributions of any additional components of \(V(K)\), proves
\eqref{eq:first-coefficient}. If \(L\) is equimultiple,
all its other coefficients vanish by Theorem~\ref{thm:AM}.
head: environment

label: lem:cyclic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cyclic}
Suppose \(g,h\) are irreducible and reduced and
\eqref{eq:normalized-power} holds. The analytic algebra
\[
C=A[z]/(z^r-g)
\]
embeds in \(B\) by \(z\mapsto h\), and \(B\) is finite over
\(C\). Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:field-degree}
[\operatorname{Frac}(B):\operatorname{Frac}(C)]=\frac d r.
\end{equation}
In particular \(r\mid d\). The finite map of reduced
hypersurfaces \(F|_{V(h)}:V(h)\to V(g)\) also has degree
\(d/r\).
head: environment
name: Cyclic factorization and degrees

title: Proof
body_md:
The ring \(A_{(g)}\) is a discrete valuation ring, and
\(z^r-g\) is Eisenstein over it. It is therefore irreducible
over \(\operatorname{Frac}(A)\), and \(C\) is a domain of rank \(r\) over
\(A\). Evaluation at \(h\) is injective: after passing to
\(\operatorname{Frac}(A)\) it is a nonzero map from a field into
\(\operatorname{Frac}(B)\). A finite set of \(A\)-module generators of
\(B\) also generates it over \(C\). The tower law now gives
\[
d=[\operatorname{Frac}(B):\operatorname{Frac}(A)]
=[\operatorname{Frac}(B):\operatorname{Frac}(C)]\,[\operatorname{Frac}(C):\operatorname{Frac}(A)],
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:field-degree}.

For the last assertion, localize the finite extension at \((g)\).
There is only one height-one prime over \((g)\), namely
\((h)\), and its ramification index is \(r\). The
free module of rank \(d\) over \(A_{(g)}\), reduced modulo
\(g\), has dimension \(d\) over the residue field. Computing
this dimension with the \(h\)-adic filtration of length \(r\)
gives
\[
d=r\,[\operatorname{Frac}(B/(h)):\operatorname{Frac}(A/(g))].
\]
The residual field degree on the right is the generic degree of
the hypersurface map. No formula involving a ratio of the
multiplicities of \(V(g)\) and \(V(h)\) is used here.
head: environment

label: thm:isolated
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:isolated}
Let \(F:(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C^n,0)\) be finite. Let \(g,h\)
be reduced equations of irreducible hypersurface germs with at most isolated singularities, where
\[
V(h)=F^{-1}(V(g))_{\mathrm{red}},\qquad
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:milnor-bound}
\mu(h)\geq\mu(g).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, \(e_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(h);B)\geqe_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(g);A)\).
Consequently all Segre numbers, and all generic L\^e numbers,
are componentwise nondecreasing. This holds for every
\(r\geq1\) in \eqref{eq:standing-power}.
head: environment
name: Jelonek's isolated-singularity comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
We give the argument of \cite[Theorem~2.2]{Jelonek} with field
coefficients explicit. Normalize as in
\eqref{eq:normalized-power}. Choose a finite proper
representative of \(F\). Choose a small target Milnor ball
\(B_\varepsilon\) and a source Milnor ball \(B'\) such that
\(F(B')\subset B_\varepsilon\). Next choose a target Milnor
ball \(B_\eta\), with \(\eta<\varepsilon\), such that
\(F^{-1}(B_\eta)\subset B'\).

For a sufficiently small nonzero \(t\), put \(c=t^r\) and
use the interiors of the corresponding Milnor fibers:
\[
M_g^- =g^{-1}(c)\cap B_\eta^{\circ},\qquad
M_g^+ =g^{-1}(c)\cap B_\varepsilon^{\circ},\qquad
M_h=h^{-1}(t)\cap (B')^{\circ}.
\]
The inclusion \(\iota:M_g^-\hookrightarrow M_g^+\) is a
homotopy equivalence. The space
\[
N=F^{-1}(M_g^-)\cap h^{-1}(t)
\]
is an open submanifold of \(M_h\), and
\(q=F|_N:N\to M_g^-\) is a nonempty finite proper map onto
the connected target. In particular it has positive degree.

A proper surjective holomorphic map between complex manifolds
of the same dimension induces an injection on cohomology with
\(\mathbb C\)-coefficients \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Wells}. Equivalently,
one may use the positive-degree transfer with rational
coefficients. Thus \(q^*\) is injective. Let
\(k=F|_{M_h}:M_h\to M_g^+\) and let \(\jmath:N\hookrightarrow M_h\)
be the inclusion. The identity
\[
\jmath^*k^*=q^*\iota^*
\]
shows that \(k^*:H^{n-1}(M_g^+;\mathbb C)\to H^{n-1}(M_h;\mathbb C)\)
is injective, since \(\iota^*\) is an isomorphism.

By Milnor's bouquet theorem \cite{Milnor}, these vector spaces
have dimensions \(\mu(g)\) and \(\mu(h)\). This proves
\eqref{eq:milnor-bound}. Notice that \(N\) itself was not
assumed to be a Milnor fiber, and no surjectivity over
\(\mathbb Z\) is required.
head: environment
name: Topological proof (Jelonek

title: Proof
body_md:
Normalize the unit and use the cyclic algebra \(C\) of
Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic}. Set
\[
A^\circ=A[1/g],\qquad C^\circ=C[1/z],\qquad B^\circ=B[1/h],
\qquad \delta=d/r.
\]
The extension \(A^\circ\subset C^\circ\) is finite \'etale,
since \(rz^{r-1}\) is invertible. Both \(C^\circ\) and
\(B^\circ\) are regular, and the finite map
\(\Phi:\operatorname{Spec} B^\circ\to\operatorname{Spec} C^\circ\) has degree \(\delta\).

For an isolated hypersurface singularity \(f\), its Brieskorn
module is
\[
\mathcal B_f=
\frac{\Omega^n_{\mathbb C^n,0}}
{df\wedge d\Omega^{n-2}_{\mathbb C^n,0}}.
\]
Here and below \(\Omega^p\) means holomorphic differential
forms, with localization when indicated. Multiplication by
\(f\) defines the action of the parameter ring \(\mathbb C\{t\}\).
The Brieskorn--Sebastiani theorem says that \(\mathcal B_f\)
is free over \(\mathbb C\{t\}\) of rank \(\mu(f)\);
see \cite[Section~1]{Sabbah}.

Write \(K_t=\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C\{t\}\), \(K_z=\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C\{z\}\), with
\(t=z^r\), and define
\[
Q_C=\frac{\Omega^n_{C^\circ}}
{dz\wedge d\Omega^{n-2}_{C^\circ}},\qquad
Q_B=\frac{\Omega^n_{B^\circ}}
{dh\wedge d\Omega^{n-2}_{B^\circ}}.
\]
These are \(K_z\)-vector spaces. Localization gives
\[
Q_B\cong\mathcal B_h\otimes_{\mathbb C\{z\}}K_z.
\]
Moreover \(C^\circ=A^\circ\otimes_{K_t}K_z\) and
\(dg=rz^{r-1}dz\). \'Etale base change for differential forms
therefore gives
\[
Q_C\cong
\bigl(\mathcal B_g\otimes_{\mathbb C\{t\}}K_t\bigr)
\otimes_{K_t}K_z.
\]
To check the denominators, observe that
\[
dg\wedge d(a(z)\eta)=a(z)\,dg\wedge d\eta,
\qquad a(z)\in K_z,
\]
because \(dg\wedge dz=0\). The same calculation justifies
localization of each Brieskorn quotient. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:brieskorn-dimensions}
\dim_{K_z}Q_C=\mu(g),\qquad\dim_{K_z}Q_B=\mu(h).
\end{equation}

For a finite map between smooth spaces, the trace on
differential forms commutes with exterior differentiation,
satisfies the projection formula, and obeys
\[
\operatorname{Tr}_\Phi\circ\Phi^*=\delta\,\mathrm{id}.
\]
These are the trace identities for the de Rham complex; see
\cite[Section~50.19]{Stacks}. In the analytic setting the trace
is the sum over inverse branches off the branch locus. It
extends holomorphically across that locus: at a generic branch
point the local model is a power map in one transverse
coordinate, where summing the branches cancels the apparent
poles; extension across the remaining codimension-two set
follows from normality. Applied to localized forms, this
construction permits poles only along the deleted divisor.
No trace on ordinary forms at the possibly singular origin of
\(C\) is asserted.

Since \(\Phi^*z=h\), pullback and trace send the respective
denominators to one another:
\begin{align*}
\Phi^*(dz\wedge d\eta)&=dh\wedge d(\Phi^*\eta),\\
\operatorname{Tr}_\Phi(dh\wedge d\xi)&=dz\wedge d(\operatorname{Tr}_\Phi\xi).
\end{align*}
They descend to \(K_z\)-linear maps
\[
Q_C\xrightarrow{\Phi^*}Q_B\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Tr}_\Phi}Q_C
\]
whose composition is \(\delta\,\mathrm{id}\). Since
\(\delta\ne0\) in characteristic zero, \(\Phi^*\) is
injective. Equation~\eqref{eq:brieskorn-dimensions} proves
\(\mu(g)\leq\mu(h)\).

Finally, Remark~\ref{rem:isolated-identification} identifies
these Milnor numbers with Hilbert--Samuel multiplicities and
the only possibly nonzero Segre and generic L\^e numbers.
This proves all the numerical conclusions of the theorem.
head: environment
name: Algebraic proof via Brieskorn modules

label: cor:isolated-degree
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: A stronger bound for reduced pullback

title: Proof
body_md:
After normalizing the unit, the chain rule gives
\(J(h)\subseteq J(g)B\). Both ideals are \(\mathfrak n\)-primary.
Monotonicity of Hilbert--Samuel multiplicity and
Lemma~\ref{lem:free} yield
\[
\mu(h)=e_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(h);B)
\geqe_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(g)B;B)=d\,e_{\mathrm{HS}}(J(g);A)=d\,\mu(g).
\]
head: environment

label: rem:isolated-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:isolated-scope}
For \(r>1\), the ideal \(h^{r-1}J(h)\) is not
\(\mathfrak n\)-primary. Thus the chain rule does not permit the
Hilbert--Samuel proof just given. The algebraic proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:isolated} instead uses Brieskorn modules and
trace; it does not establish a factor \(d\), or \(d/r\),
in \eqref{eq:milnor-bound}.

Both proofs of \eqref{eq:milnor-bound} also apply to reduced,
not necessarily irreducible, \(g,h\) with isolated critical
points, provided the single-power identity
\(g\circ F=uh^r\) is assumed. In the algebraic proof,
Eisenstein may be applied at any irreducible factor of the
reduced germ \(g\). In the topological proof the Milnor
fibers are still connected. This observation will be useful
for transversal slices, which need not be irreducible.
head: environment
name: Scope of the algebraic argument

label: cormain-theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cormain-theorem} Let $({\bf V},0)\subset (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ be a germ of a complex hypersurface and let $F: (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ be a germ of a finite holomorphic mapping. Then if the germ $(F^{-1}({\bf V}),0)$ taken with the reduced structure is smooth, then also the germ 
$({\bf V}, 0)$ is smooth.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction with respect to $n.$ Note that if  ${\bf V}$ has an isolated singularity, then it  is smooth if and only if $\mu({\bf V})=0$. In particular in this case  our theorem follows directly from Theorem \ref{thm:isolated}. 
In particular we get the thesis if  $n=2.$  

Now assume that $n>2$ and ${\bf S}:=Sing({\bf V},0)$ has dimension greater than $0.$ Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a linear system of hyperplanes in $\mathbb{C}^n.$ On $V$ let us consider the induced linear system $\mathcal{L}_V$. 
Then a generic member $L_V$ of $\mathcal{L}_V$ is singular, because $S\cap L\not=\emptyset$ (see Lemma 2.5 in \cite{j-b}). Moreover $F^*(L_V)$ (and $F^{-1}(L)$) are  smooth because the system $F^*(\mathcal{L}_V)$ has no base points on smooth $W=F^{-1}(V)\subset F^{-1}(L)$ (the system $F^*(\mathcal{L})$ has no base points on $\mathbb{C}^n$). Since dim $L< n$, this is a contradiction.
head: environment

label: thm:reduced-lex
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Lexicographic monotonicity for reduced pullback

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:chain-rule} and Theorem~\ref{thm:ideal-lex},
\(\mathbf e(K;B)\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbf e(I;B)\).
Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-segre} gives the componentwise inequalities
\(e_j(I;B)\geq e_j(J;A)\), and hence
\(\mathbf e(I;B)\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbf e(J;A)\).
Transitivity proves \eqref{eq:reduced-lex}; then apply
\eqref{eq:le-segre-c}.
head: environment

label: prop:top-dimensional
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:top-dimensional}
Assume \eqref{eq:reduced-hypothesis} and
\(\dim\Sigma(g)=\dim\Sigma(h)=s\). Then all coefficients
\(c_i(J(g))\) and \(c_i(J(h))\) with \(i>s\) vanish, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:s-sandwich}
c_s(J(h);B)\geq c_s(I;B)\geq c_s(J(g);A).
\end{equation}
In Segre and L\^e notation this gives
\[
e_{n-s}(J(h))\geq e_{n-s}(J(g)),\qquad
\lambda^{s}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{s}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g).
\]
head: environment
name: The highest-dimensional singular contribution

title: Proof
body_md:
Finiteness and faithful flatness give \(\dim B/I=s\).
The vanishing follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:AM}.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:first-coefficient} to \(K\subseteq I\)
for the first inequality in \eqref{eq:s-sandwich}, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-segre} for the second.
head: environment

label: thm:equimultiple
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:equimultiple}
Assume
\[
g\circ F=uh,\qquad
\dim\Sigma(g)=\dim\Sigma(h)=s,
\qquad \ell(J(g))=\operatorname{ht} J(g)=n-s.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equimultiple-componentwise}
e_j(J(h);B)\geq e_j(J(g);A),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equimultiple-le}
\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g),\qquad 0\leq i\leq n-1.
\end{equation}
No equimultiplicity assumption on \(J(h)\) is necessary.
If \(J(h)\) is also equimultiple, both multiplicity sequences
are supported only at index \(s\).
head: environment
name: Equimultiple target in arbitrary singular dimension

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:AM} gives \(c_i(J(g))=0\) for \(i\ne s\).
At index \(s\), Proposition~\ref{prop:top-dimensional}
gives the required inequality. At every other index,
nonnegativity of \(c_i(J(h))\) suffices. Equations
\eqref{eq:segre-c} and \eqref{eq:le-segre-c} translate the result.
If \(J(h)\) is equimultiple, apply the same vanishing theorem
to that ideal.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The intermediate ideal \(I=JB\) has the same
analytic spread as \(J\). Indeed, flatness identifies
\[
I^k/\mathfrak n I^k\cong J^k/\mathfrak m J^k
\]
for every \(k\), compatibly with products. Thus the special
fiber rings are isomorphic over \(\mathbb C\). In particular,
equimultiplicity of \(J\) implies equimultiplicity of \(I\),
but not of the smaller ideal \(K\).
head: environment
name: Analytic spread under finite-flat extension

label: thm:curve-equality
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: An equality criterion in singular dimension one

title: Proof
body_md:
Equations \eqref{eq:curve-sandwich} and \eqref{eq:curve-lex}
follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:top-dimensional} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:reduced-lex}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:ideal-lex}
to \(K\subseteq I\). All earlier Segre coordinates vanish.
If \(c_1(K)=c_1(I)\), lexicographic monotonicity therefore
forces
\[
c_0(K)\geq c_0(I)=d\,c_0(J),
\]
where the last equality is \eqref{eq:j-degree}.
head: environment

label: cor:curve-cases
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Componentwise cases in singular dimension one

title: Proof
body_md:
In case (1), \eqref{eq:curve-sandwich} forces
\(c_1(K)=c_1(I)\), so Theorem~\ref{thm:curve-equality} applies.
In case (2), \(c_0(J)=0\) by Theorem~\ref{thm:AM}; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:equimultiple} and nonnegativity.

In case (3), at a prime \(\mathfrak q\) defining a curve
component of \(\Sigma(h)\), the matrix \(DF\) is invertible
over \(B_{\mathfrak q}\). The chain rule gives
\(K B_{\mathfrak q}=I B_{\mathfrak q}\). Consequently
\(K\) and \(I\) have the same curve components and the same
local multiplicities on them. Formula~\eqref{eq:AM-assoc}
gives \(c_1(K)=c_1(I)\), and
Theorem~\ref{thm:curve-equality} applies.

For the last assertion, write \(g\circ F=uh^r\). At a point
of \(V(h)\) outside \(R_F\), the map is a local
biholomorphism and the pullback of a reduced divisor is reduced.
Condition (3) supplies such points arbitrarily close to the
origin. Since \(V(h)\) is irreducible, the exponent \(r\)
is constant along it, and hence \(r=1\).
head: environment

label: rem:curve-gap
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:curve-gap}
If \(c_1(K)>c_1(I)\), lexicographic monotonicity for
\(K\subseteq I\) imposes no inequality on \(c_0(K)\).
In particular, \eqref{eq:curve-lex} alone does not prove
\(\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)\). This is the remaining
coordinate in singular dimension one outside the cases above.
head: environment
name: What lexicographic comparison leaves open

title: Remark
body_md:
For an ideal \(Q\) with \(\dim R/Q=1\),
\cite[Theorem~3(4)]{AM} gives
\[
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(G_Q(R))=c_0(Q;R)+c_1(Q;R),
\]
where the multiplicity is taken at the homogeneous maximal
ideal of the associated graded ring. Thus, for two such
ideals \(K,L\), the assertion \(c_0(K)\geq c_0(L)\) is
equivalent to
\[
e_{\mathrm{HS}}(G_K(R))-e_{\mathrm{HS}}(G_L(R))\geq c_1(K)-c_1(L).
\]
This is a useful reformulation, not an additional monotonicity
theorem: the required lower bound on the left still needs proof.
head: environment
name: The total associated-graded multiplicity

label: prop:ILM
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ILM}
Let \(g,h\) have one-dimensional critical loci, and choose
generic coordinates \(\mathbf z\) for \(g\) and
\(\mathbf w\) for \(h\). Suppose that, for all sufficiently
large integers \(N\), isolated perturbations satisfying the
L\^e--Iomdine formula also satisfy
\[
\mu(h+b_N w_1^N)\geq\mu(g+a_N z_1^N),
\qquad a_N,b_N\ne0.
\]
Then
\[
(\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h),\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h))
\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}(\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g),\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)).
\]
head: environment
name: A conditional reduction using isolated perturbations

title: Proof
body_md:
The L\^e--Iomdine formula \cite[Theorem~3.5]{Massey24},
for sufficiently large exponents and suitable nonzero
coefficients, gives
\[
\mu(f+a_N z_1^N)=\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f)+(N-1)\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f).
\]
Subtract the formulas for \(h\) and \(g\). Nonnegativity
for arbitrarily large \(N\) first implies
\(\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)\). If these entries agree,
it also implies \(\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)\).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The perturbation inequality in Proposition~\ref{prop:ILM}
is an additional hypothesis. The two perturbations need not
be related by a finite pullback, even when \(g\) and \(h\)
are. Also, the pullback of a generic linear coordinate can
have zero differential at the origin. Therefore this
proposition does not prove the missing componentwise case.
head: environment

label: cor:prepolar
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:prepolar}
Assume \eqref{eq:curve-hypothesis}, and assume that \(J(g)\)
is equimultiple. Let \(\mathbf z\) be prepolar for \(g\),
with \(\delta_g(\mathbf z)=0\), and let \(\mathbf w\) be
any prepolar system for \(h\). Then
\[
\lambda^i_{h,\mathbf w}(0)\geq\lambda^i_{g,\mathbf z}(0),
\qquad i=0,1.
\]
head: environment
name: A prepolar comparison with zero target excess

title: Proof
body_md:
Equimultiplicity gives \(\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)=0\); by
\eqref{eq:prepolar-excess} and \(\delta_g(\mathbf z)=0\),
\(\lambda^0_{g,\mathbf z}(0)=0\) and
\(\lambda^1_{g,\mathbf z}(0)=\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)\).
The index-zero inequality follows from nonnegativity. For
index one, use \eqref{eq:prepolar-excess} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:top-dimensional}:
\[
\lambda^1_{h,\mathbf w}(0)\geq\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)
\geq\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)=\lambda^1_{g,\mathbf z}(0).
\]
head: environment

label: prop:transversal
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Transversal comparison and pushforward

title: Proof
body_md:
Restriction to the compatible slices gives
\[
(g|_{T_q})\circ(F|_{S_p})=(u|_{S_p})(h|_{S_p})^r.
\]
Apply the isolated comparison in the reduced, possibly
reducible, form explained in Remark~\ref{rem:isolated-scope}.
This proves \eqref{eq:transverse-mu}.

Let \(d_\beta\geq1\) be the generic degree of the finite
curve map \(D_\beta\to C_\alpha\). Formula
\eqref{eq:intrinsic-le-cycle} yields
\[
F_*\Lambda_h^1=
\sum_\alpha\left(
\sum_{F(D_\beta)=C_\alpha}
d_\beta\mu_{D_\beta}^\perp(h)\right)[C_\alpha]+E,
\]
where \(E\) is the effective cycle contributed by components
whose images are not components of \(\Sigma(g)\). By
condition (1), each inner sum is nonempty; by
\eqref{eq:transverse-mu}, its coefficient is at least
\(\mu_{C_\alpha}^\perp(g)\). This proves
\eqref{eq:cycle-pushforward}.

Choose \(L\) general enough to meet every image curve
properly and to compute \(\operatorname{mult}_0\Lambda_g^1\). The
projection formula for finite maps gives
\[
\bigl(\Lambda_h^1\cdot V(L\circ F)\bigr)_0
=\bigl(F_*\Lambda_h^1\cdot V(L)\bigr)_0,
\]
because the germ of \(F^{-1}(0)\) is supported at the origin.
Now use \eqref{eq:cycle-pushforward}.
head: environment

label: cor:transversal-origin
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: An additional condition at the origin

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows from \eqref{eq:pullback-cut}
and \eqref{eq:cut-realizes-multiplicity}. Equimultiplicity
of \(J(g)\) makes \(\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)=0\); all other indices
except one vanish. Nonnegativity proves the second assertion.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
A sufficient condition for \eqref{eq:cut-realizes-multiplicity}
is that the linear part of \(L\circ F\) be general for the
tangent cone of \(\Lambda_h^1\). Finiteness alone does not
ensure this. In general \(L\circ F\) is neither a linear
form nor a local coordinate, and its intersection with the
source cycle may exceed the cycle multiplicity. Therefore
\eqref{eq:cycle-pushforward} and \eqref{eq:pullback-cut}
alone do not compare the generic L\^e numbers at the origin.
The compatible smooth slices in condition (2) are also genuine
extra hypotheses, not an automatic property of a finite map.
head: environment
name: Why the extra condition is essential to the argument

label: ex:equimultiple
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:equimultiple}
Fix \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq s\leq n-2\), and put \(m=n-s\).
With \(s\) additional variables \(\mathbf z\), let
\begin{align*}
g(\mathbf x,\mathbf z)&=x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_{m-1}^2+x_m^3,\\
F(\mathbf u,\mathbf w)&=(u_1^2,u_2,\ldots,u_m,\mathbf w),\\
h(\mathbf u,\mathbf w)&=u_1^4+u_2^2+\cdots+u_{m-1}^2+u_m^3.
\end{align*}
Then \(d=2\), \(g\circ F=h\), and both hypersurfaces are
irreducible. For \(m=2\) this follows from the coprime
exponent pairs \((2,3)\), \((4,3)\); for \(m>2\) it follows
because the transverse hypersurfaces have isolated singularities
and dimension at least two. Both singular loci are smooth of
dimension \(s\).

The Jacobian ideals are complete intersections of height \(m\):
\[
J(g)=(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1},x_m^2),\qquad
J(h)=(u_1^3,u_2,\ldots,u_{m-1},u_m^2).
\]
They are equimultiple. The transverse quotient lengths are
\(2\) and \(6\), while the singular-locus multiplicities are
one. Theorem~\ref{thm:AM} gives
\[
c_s(J(g))=2,\qquad c_s(J(h))=6,
\qquad c_i(J(g))=c_i(J(h))=0\quad(i\ne s).
\]
Thus \(\lambda^{s}_{\mathrm{gen}}\) increases from \(2\) to \(6\), and all
other generic L\^e numbers vanish. If \(s>0\), the entire
singular locus upstairs lies in \(R_F=V(u_1)\). This example
is covered by the equimultiple theorem, not by the
nonramification condition of Corollary~\ref{cor:curve-cases}.
head: environment
name: Equimultiple examples in every singular dimension

label: ex:tangential-degree
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:tangential-degree}
In \(\mathbb C^3\), take
\[
g(x,y,z)=x^2+y^3,\qquad F(u,v,w)=(u,v,w^d),\qquad d>1.
\]
The reduced pullback is \(h=u^2+v^3\), so
\[
\mathbf e(J(g))=\mathbf e(J(h))=(0,2,0),\qquad
(\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}},\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}})=(2,0).
\]
Both hypersurfaces are irreducible and both singular loci are
one-dimensional. Thus neither a factor \(d\) nor a factor
\(d/r\) can be inserted in every coordinate of the proposed
nonisolated comparison: here \(r=1\) and that factor would
require \(2\geq2d\). Adding unused variables gives the same
phenomenon in higher singular-locus dimension.
head: environment
name: Degree can occur entirely in the singular direction

label: ex:quartic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:quartic}
Consider
\[
g(x,y,z)=x^4+y^4-xyz,\qquad
F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z^2),\qquad
h(x,y,z)=x^4+y^4-xyz^2.
\]
Then \(d=2\), \(g\circ F=h\), and
\(\Sigma(g)=\Sigma(h)=V(x,y)\). At a general point of this
axis, each transverse singularity is a node, so its Milnor
number is one. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quartic-first}
\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g)=\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)=1.
\end{equation}

Both equations are irreducible. For \(g\), a factorization
would have a factor of order one, with initial form \(x\),
\(y\), or \(z\), because its initial form is \(-xyz\).
An implicit solution \(x=\varphi(y,z)\) with
\(\operatorname{ord}\varphi\geq2\) contradicts
\(\varphi(y,0)^4+y^4=0\); the \(y\)-case is identical.
An implicit solution for \(z\) would require
\(x^4+y^4\) to be divisible by \(xy\), which it is not.
For \(h\), regard it as a primitive quadratic in \(z\):
\((x^4+y^4)/(xy)\) is not a square in \(\mathbb C(x,y)\), since
its valuation at \(x\) is odd. Hence \(h\) is irreducible
as a homogeneous polynomial and therefore as an analytic germ.

The remaining numbers can be computed explicitly from L\^e
cycles with first coordinate \(z\). For \(g\), the residual
polar curve is the union of four reduced curves
\[
y=\zeta x,\qquad z=4\zeta^{-1}x^2,\qquad \zeta^4=1.
\]
Along each curve, \(g_z=-xy\) has order two, giving
\(\lambda^0_{g,(z,x,y)}(0)=8\). For \(h\), the residual
polar curve consists of eight reduced lines
\[
y=\zeta x,\qquad z^2=4\zeta^{-1}x^2,\qquad \zeta^4=1.
\]
On each line \(h_z=-2xyz\) has order three, giving
\(\lambda^0_{h,(z,x,y)}(0)=24\).

These coordinate choices are prepolar: their first slices are
\(x^4+y^4\), with isolated critical point. The coordinate
\(z\) meets the singular axis with multiplicity one, so the
excess in \eqref{eq:coordinate-excess} is zero. Thus the
computed numbers are the generic values, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quartic-numbers}
\mathbf e(J(g))=(0,1,8),\qquad
\mathbf e(J(h))=(0,1,24).
\end{equation}
In particular, both ideals have maximal analytic spread, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:curve-cases}(1) applies. This example
illustrates a componentwise case beyond equimultiplicity.
head: environment
name: A non-equimultiple pair with one-dimensional singular locus

label: ex:prepolar-counterexample
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:prepolar-counterexample}
For \(k\geq2\), let
\[
f(x,y,z)=(x-z^k)^2+y^3.
\]
It is an irreducible reduced germ, analytically equivalent to
a cusp times a line. Its Jacobian ideal and singular locus are
\[
J(f)=(x-z^k,y^2),\qquad
C=\Sigma(f)=V(x-z^k,y).
\]
The ideal is equimultiple, \(C\) is smooth, and the
transverse Milnor number is two. Hence
\[
(\lambda^{1}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f),\lambda^{0}_{\mathrm{gen}}(f))=(2,0).
\]

The linear coordinate systems \(\mathbf z=(x,y,z)\) and
\(\mathbf w=(z,y,x)\) are prepolar. Their first slices are
respectively \(z^{2k}+y^3\) and \(x^2+y^3\), both with
isolated critical point. For \(\mathbf z\),
\[
\Lambda^1_{f,\mathbf z}=2[C],\qquad
\Gamma^1_{f,\mathbf z}=2(k-1)[V(y,z)].
\]
Intersecting the first cycle with \(V(x)\), and the second
with \(V(f_x)\), gives
\[
(\lambda^1_{f,\mathbf z}(0),\lambda^0_{f,\mathbf z}(0))
=(2k,2k-2).
\]
For \(\mathbf w\), the residual polar curve vanishes and
the corresponding pair is \((2,0)\).

Taking \(F=\mathrm{id}\), \(g=h=f\), using \(\mathbf z\)
on the target and \(\mathbf w\) on the source, disproves a
comparison asserted for \emph{arbitrary} prepolar choices.
It does not contradict the generic formulation: the two
generic vectors are equal.
head: environment
name: Prepolar values need not be generic values

label: rem:power-ideal
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:power-ideal}
There is no general identity
\(c_i(h^{r-1}J(h))=r\,c_i(J(h))\). For example, in
\(\mathbb C^2\) let \(h=x^2+y^3\) and \(r\geq2\). Since
\(J(h)=(x,y^2)\) is primary, \(e_1(J(h))=0\). But the
divisorial Segre cycle of \(h^{r-1}J(h)\) is
\((r-1)[V(h)]\), so
\[
e_1(h^{r-1}J(h))=2(r-1)>0.
\]
This is why the factor \(h^{r-1}\) in the chain rule
cannot be removed by a uniform rescaling of the multiplicity
sequence.
head: environment
name: Multiplying the Jacobian ideal by a power of its equation

label: conj:segre-monotonicity
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:segre-monotonicity}
Let \(F:(\mathbb C^n,0)\to(\mathbb C^n,0)\) be finite, and let
\(V=V(g)\) be a singular irreducible reduced hypersurface.
Suppose \(W=F^{-1}(V)_{\mathrm{red}}\) is irreducible and
let \(h\) be a reduced equation for \(W\). Then
\[
e_j(J(h);\mathbb C^n)\geq e_j(J(g);\mathbb C^n),\qquad 1\leq j\leq n.
\]
head: environment
name: Componentwise Segre monotonicity

label: conj:le-monotonicity
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:le-monotonicity}
Under the hypotheses of Conjecture~\ref{conj:segre-monotonicity},
\[
\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(h)\geq\lambda^{i}_{\mathrm{gen}}(g),\qquad 0\leq i\leq n-1.
\]
head: environment
name: Equivalent generic L\^e formulation

label: conj:ramified-lex
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:ramified-lex}
Under the hypotheses of Conjecture~\ref{conj:segre-monotonicity},
\[
\mathbf e(J(h))\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbf e(J(g)).
\]
head: environment
name: Lexicographic comparison with arbitrary ramification
